title: Draw a flowchart to calculate and print the sum of all even numbers between 20 and 40 (both inclusive). Start, initialize sum = 0 and i = 20, loop while i <= 40 doing sum = sum + i, i = i + 2, print sum, End. Input: none, Expected Output: 330.
shortTitle: Sum of Even Numbers between 20 and 40 — print their total

s1_definition.profdef: This sums an arithmetic series of even numbers over a bounded range by starting at the first even value, twenty, and stepping by two up to forty, adding each term. Because every term is even by construction, no filtering is needed. The closed form for an arithmetic series, the count of terms times the average of the first and last term, gives the same total directly.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India sums the processing fees charged on even-numbered account tiers from tier twenty to tier forty, where only even tiers carry a fee. The system starts at twenty and adds every second tier up to forty, giving a total of three hundred thirty. The same total comes instantly from counting the terms and multiplying by their average.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sum even numbers in a range by starting at the first even value and stepping by two, or use the arithmetic-series formula of term count times the average of the first and last term.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This sums an arithmetic series of even numbers over a bounded range by starting at the first even value, twenty, and stepping by two up to forty, adding each term. Because every term is even by construction, no filtering is needed. The closed form for an arithmetic series, the count of terms times the average of the first and last term, gives the same total directly.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India sums the processing fees charged on even-numbered account tiers from tier twenty to tier forty, where only even tiers carry a fee. The system starts at twenty and adds every second tier up to forty, giving a total of three hundred thirty. The same total comes instantly from counting the terms and multiplying by their average.

**One line to remember:** Sum even numbers in a range by starting at the first even value and stepping by two, or use the arithmetic-series formula of term count times the average of the first and last term.

sections.s2_technical:
The loop version seeds the total at zero and the counter at twenty, then adds the counter and steps it by two while it stays at or below forty. Because it starts on an even boundary and steps by two, every value added is even, so there is no per-element modulo test. The terms are twenty, twenty-two, twenty-four, and so on up to forty, and their total is three hundred thirty.

The arithmetic-series closed form is the senior insight. For an evenly spaced series the sum equals the number of terms times the average of the first and last terms. Here the terms run from twenty to forty in steps of two. The number of terms is forty minus twenty, divided by two, plus one, which is eleven. The average of the first and last is twenty plus forty over two, which is thirty. Eleven times thirty is three hundred thirty, matching the loop. This computes in constant time regardless of the range size.

Choosing the step correctly is the key correctness point: starting at the first even value and stepping by two is cleaner and faster than iterating every integer and filtering with a modulo test. For money I would accumulate with BigDecimal and compute the formula with exact arithmetic to avoid overflow and drift. A senior nuance is to be careful with the inclusive bounds, since both twenty and forty are included, so the term count uses plus one, and an off-by-one there is the most common mistake in range-sum problems, which the closed form makes explicit and easy to verify against the loop.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India sums fees across even-numbered account tiers from twenty to forty inclusive. We must add the even numbers in that range. This is exactly the start-at-twenty, step-by-two accumulation.

Problem 2 — Iterating every tier and filtering would double the work. This is exactly why we step by two and touch only even tiers.

Problem 3 — The inclusive bounds make an off-by-one easy, so we verify the total two ways. This is exactly why we also compute the arithmetic-series closed form.

Our mini-project builds a `RangeEvenSum` with a `sumEvens(int lo, int hi)` loop method and a `sumEvensFormula(int lo, int hi)` closed-form method, and a `SumEvensRangeDemo` runnable that shows both give three hundred thirty for twenty to forty.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: none; the range is fixed from twenty to forty inclusive.

Step 1 — The loop seeds the total at zero and the counter at twenty, which is already even, so start is twenty.

Step 2 — The loop adds twenty, then steps to twenty-two and adds it, then twenty-four, and so on, adding only even values because the step is two.

Step 3 — It continues adding twenty-six, twenty-eight, thirty, thirty-two, thirty-four, thirty-six, thirty-eight, and finally forty, after which the counter becomes forty-two and the loop stops.

Step 4 — The running total of twenty through forty in steps of two is three hundred thirty.

Step 5 — The formula method computes the first even as twenty, the last even as forty, the term count as forty minus twenty over two plus one, which is eleven, and the average as twenty plus forty over two, which is thirty, giving eleven times thirty equals three hundred thirty. Both results agree and are logged.

Final output:

```
2026-11-01 00:10:00 [INFO] Even tier fee sum 20..40 via loop    = 330
2026-11-01 00:10:00 [INFO] Even tier fee sum 20..40 via formula = 330
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Range: 20..40 inclusive, even only
    │
    ├─ LOOP (start 20, step 2):       ├─ FORMULA:
    │  20+22+24+...+40                 │  first=20, last=40
    │  running → 330                   │  terms=(40-20)/2+1 = 11
    │                                  │  avg=(20+40)/2 = 30
    ▼                                  │  11 × 30 = 330
  330 (both paths agree)               ▼
```

```
  1. sumEvens(20,40) → 330
  2. sumEvensFormula(20,40):

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Summing the even numbers between twenty and forty inclusive is an arithmetic-series sum over a stepped range. The loop version seeds a total at zero, starts the counter at twenty, and steps by two up to forty, adding each value, so it only ever touches even numbers and never needs a modulo test. The terms twenty, twenty-two, up to forty sum to three hundred thirty.

The senior insight is the closed form for an arithmetic series: the sum equals the number of terms times the average of the first and last term. Here the first even is twenty and the last is forty, the number of terms is forty minus twenty divided by two plus one, which is eleven, and the average of first and last is thirty, so the sum is eleven times thirty, three hundred thirty, computed in constant time regardless of how wide the range is. The detail I watch most carefully is the inclusive bounds, because both twenty and forty are included, so the term count needs the plus one, and that off-by-one is the single most common mistake in range-sum problems, which is exactly why I verify the loop and the formula against each other.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I applied this to roll up fees across even-numbered account tiers from tier twenty to tier forty, where only even tiers carried a fee. I wrote a RangeEvenSum class with a loop that starts on the first even boundary and steps by two, and a closed-form method that uses term count times the average of the first and last term, guarding against an empty range and the off-by-one on inclusive bounds. Both produced three hundred thirty. The lesson I emphasize is that stepping by two beats filtering with modulo, and that knowing the arithmetic-series formula lets you replace the loop entirely and cross-check the inclusive-bound arithmetic that trips people up.
